name: The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms
title: The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms
answer: The AI enablement audit is a structured review of whether an investment firm can actually use artificial intelligence safely, not just whether it has bought or built any. It covers the models in production, the data feeding them, the people who operate and check them, and the controls around their output. The audit treats enablement as a chain: a model that works but cannot be explained, monitored or reproduced is not enabled in any useful sense. It sits within governance and fiduciary risk because the firm's duty to clients does not change when a process is automated.

sections.body: The AI enablement audit is a structured review of whether an investment firm can actually use artificial intelligence safely, not just whether it has bought or built any. It covers the models in production, the data feeding them, the people who operate and check them, and the controls around their output. The audit treats enablement as a chain: a model that works but cannot be explained, monitored or reproduced is not enabled in any useful sense. It sits within governance and fiduciary risk because the firm's duty to clients does not change when a process is automated.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The audit runs on the firm's own record of what is deployed and where. That means an inventory of models and vendors, data lineage from source systems to training and inference, access logs, and the change history of any model or prompt in use. It also draws on the surrounding stack: cloud or on-premise compute, the data warehouse, the model registry, and the monitoring and alerting tools already in place for trading and operations. Where third party models are used through an API, the contract, the data processing terms and the version pinning are part of the evidence base.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work begins with scoping: which models touch client money, client data or investment decisions, and which are internal aids. Each in-scope model is then walked through its lifecycle, from the business case and data sources to validation, deployment, monitoring and retirement. Reviewers test reproducibility, look for undocumented manual overrides, and check that outputs can be traced back to inputs and to a named owner. Findings are graded by the size of the gap and the exposure it creates, and remediation is tracked to closure rather than left as a list of recommendations.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The audit produces evidence for the firm's own risk committee, its compliance function and, where relevant, its regulator. It tests whether accountability is assigned to a person rather than a team or a tool, whether model risk policy covers AI specifically, and whether client disclosures match what is actually done with client data. Provenance matters throughout: where training data came from, what consent or licence covers it, and whether a model's output can be defended after the fact. Records must survive staff turnover, vendor changes and model retraining, which is often where firms are weakest.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect the audit to move from periodic exercise to continuous monitoring, with model inventories and control checks wired into the same systems that run the models. Regulatory expectations are converging on documented ownership, explainability and testing for bias and drift, and firms that treat the audit as a one-off filing will find the gap widening. The harder shift is cultural: getting investment teams to see the audit as part of how a model earns its place, rather than a hurdle placed in front of it. Vendors will face more questions about model versions, data use and change notification, and contracts will follow.
